newsitem.title: TURKEY: No shortage despite Turk refinery stoppage-Tupras.
newsitem.headline: No shortage despite Turk refinery stoppage-Tupras.

text.p: Turkey's private Atas oil refinery will stop production from midnight in a pricing dispute with the government, but state-run Tupras said it could easily step in and prevent any shortage of petroleum products.

"The production will stop this midnight. Our purpose is not to liquidate our business. We hope problems with the government are to be solved," Bulent Pasin, head of Atas' administration department, told Reuters.

Atas, owned by Mobil Corp, Royal Dutch/Shell Group, British Petroleum Co Plc and Turkish Marmara Petrol, blamed the decision on increasing losses due to the government's pricing policy and urged a new pricing mechanism.

The refinery's partners said the production stoppage at the refinery, which accounts for 14 percent of Turkish production of petroleum products, might cause shortages in southern Turkey where it is based.

But a statement from Turkey's giant state-run Tupras said Atas' market share had fallen to seven percent since end-September due to a gradual reduction in output, adding the effect of the stoppage would be negligible.
"(The stopage) will not create a significiant shortage in the market and the gap can easily be met by our company," Tupras general manager Ergun Kuran said in a statement.

Tupras refined 23 million tonnes of crude oil (roughly 460,000 barrels per day) last year at its four plants, compared with 4.03 million tonnes (some 80,000 bpd) refined at the Atas plant in the Mediterranean port town of Mersin, according to figures from the Turkish energy ministry.
Tupras used 83 percent of its total refining capacity of 27.6 million tonnes (552,000 bpd) last year and Atas 91.6 percent of its 4.4-million-tonne (88,000 bpd) capacity, the figures showed.
"The distributor companies, owned by the Atas partners, have a 23 percent share in Turkey and Tupras has been supplying 55 percent of the petroleum products they sell," Kuran said.
Atas, which said the production stopage would continue until "a workable system for fuel pricing is introduced" would not lay off any workers, Pasin said.
Atas' total 1996 loss has reached $55 million after $43 million in 1995.
The Atas partners said the company could operate at a breakeven point if the government raises fuel prices by 40 percent.

"Studies continue between various levels of the state and our company to solve developments in international markets which negatively affect costs. I hope a solution will be reached soon," Kuran of Tupras said.
He did not give any further details.

Atas has proposed the government switch to "a roboust Automatic Pricing Mechanism which would ensure that the price of refined products would take account of the costs of the raw materials involved and the cost of production."
